panels:
SOLID was assembled by Robert C. Martin around 2000 (the acronym was coined later by Michael Feathers) from older ideas: Bertrand Meyer's open/closed principle (1988) and Barbara Liskov's 1987 substitution talk. All five target one cost: the price of change. A design is good when a typical change touches few files, needs little retesting and cannot break unrelated features.

The principles overlap. Dependency inversion is the usual mechanism that makes open/closed possible; interface segregation is single responsibility applied to interfaces; Liskov substitution is the rule that keeps polymorphism, and therefore open/closed, honest. In Python, many of them map onto lighter tools than class hierarchies: first-class functions, typing.Protocol for structural typing, and modules as natural units of responsibility. Interviewers rarely want definitions recited; they want you to spot the violation in a snippet and name the smallest fix.

Martin's refined wording is that a module should be responsible to one actor: one group of people who request changes. Report mixing totals and PDF layout serves two actors, finance and design, so their requests collide in one file and in one merge conflict.

Responsibility is not 'does one thing' at the line level; a class with ten methods can still have a single responsibility if all of them change together. The useful signals are change history (files that always change for different tickets), test setup (needing a printer mock to test arithmetic) and naming trouble (Manager, Helper, Util). Over-applying SRP produces anemic classes and scattered logic, which raises the cost of following a feature. Cohesion is the counterweight: keep together what changes together, separate what changes for different reasons.

Meyer's original version used inheritance: a published class is closed, and you extend it by subclassing. The modern version uses polymorphism over an abstraction: callers depend on pay(), and new behavior arrives as a new implementation registered somewhere, such as a dict of handlers, an entry-point plugin or a strategy passed in.

No code is closed against every change. You choose the axis of variation you expect, for example new payment methods, and you remain open to edits on other axes. Guessing wrong creates indirection with no payoff, which is why a common rule is to introduce the extension point on the second or third variation, not the first. A Python match statement over a closed set of cases is fine; an if/elif on type that is copied into five functions is the smell.

Liskov and Wing formalized it as behavioral subtyping: a subtype may not strengthen preconditions, may not weaken postconditions, must preserve the base type's invariants, and must respect the history constraint (it cannot allow state changes the base forbids). Type checkers verify signatures, not these behavioral promises, so LSP violations pass mypy and fail in production.

Square/Rectangle breaks because the base promises that set_width leaves height unchanged. Fixes include making shapes immutable (with_width returns a new object), or dropping the inheritance and sharing a Shape protocol with area(). Typical real violations: a subclass that raises NotImplementedError, returns None where a list was promised, demands extra setup, or narrows accepted argument types. Python's collections.abc is a good model: Sequence promises read-only behavior and MutableSequence extends it, never the reverse.

Fat interfaces force implementers to stub methods they cannot support and force clients to recompile or retest when unrelated methods change. In statically typed languages the recompilation cost was the original motivation; in Python the cost is mostly conceptual coupling and misleading APIs that raise at runtime.

typing.Protocol fits ISP well: a function can declare that it needs only something with print(), and any object with that method satisfies it without inheriting anything. Define interfaces from the client's side (what this caller needs) rather than from the implementer's side (everything the class can do). The split can go too far: dozens of single-method protocols scattered across modules are hard to discover. A role interface per client group, such as Readable versus Writable storage, is the usual sweet spot.

Dependency inversion has two parts: high-level policy should not depend on low-level detail, and both should depend on an abstraction owned by the high-level side. Ownership is the subtle bit: the Repo interface belongs next to OrderService, so the domain package does not import the database package; the database adapter imports the domain instead. That inversion of the import arrow is what gives the principle its name, and it is the core of hexagonal (ports and adapters) and clean architecture.

Dependency injection is the usual technique, but not the same thing: you can inject concrete classes and still depend on details. In Python, DI is usually just constructor parameters with sensible defaults, wired once in main(); heavy containers are rarely needed. Watch for leaky abstractions, such as a repo interface that exposes SQL strings, which keeps the coupling in disguise.

Every abstraction has a cost: more files, more indirection, and code that is harder to follow in a debugger or code review. The trade only pays off where change actually happens. Two useful heuristics: the rule of three (abstract on the third variation) and 'make the change easy, then make the easy change' (Kent Beck), which says to refactor toward a principle at the moment a real change needs it.

Legitimate reasons to bend: throwaway scripts and prototypes, performance-critical inner loops where virtual dispatch or allocation matters, data classes that are simply records, and frameworks that impose their own structure (for example Django models mixing data and persistence by design). Some argue that SOLID is less central in functional or data-oriented code, where pure functions and simple data already give low coupling. Know the principles well enough to explain why you are deviating.

The Penguin case is a textbook LSP failure: the base class promises fly() works, and a subtype breaks that promise. It also hints at an ISP issue, because Bird bundles a capability not every bird has. The fix models capabilities separately: a Bird base with shared traits, and a FlyingBird subtype or a CanFly protocol for flying behavior.

Interview follow-ups often add twists. If you add Ostrich and Kiwi, does your hierarchy still hold? (Capabilities scale better than deep trees.) If fly() must exist on all birds for legacy callers, can returning False be acceptable? Only if the base contract documents that fly() may fail; changing the contract is a breaking API change. Another classic: should Stack inherit from list? No, because list exposes insert() at any index, which breaks the stack's invariant; compose a list inside instead.
swe-design-01.further: Read Martin's Clean Architecture for the actor-based SRP and dependency rule, and Liskov and Wing's 1994 paper 'A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping' for the formal contract rules. Explore hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters), design by contract, and Python's typing.Protocol and abc modules. GRASP principles (information expert, low coupling, high cohesion) and the coupling/cohesion vocabulary give a complementary lens. For balance, look at critiques arguing for simpler data-oriented or functional designs, and at CUPID, an alternative set of properties proposed by Dan North.

panels:
The Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides) published Design Patterns in 1994 with 23 patterns in three families: creational (5), structural (7) and behavioral (11). Creational patterns all answer one question: who decides which concrete class gets instantiated, and when?

In languages where classes are first-class objects, like Python, several patterns collapse into simple idioms. A class is already a factory (call it), a dict mapping names to classes is a registry, functools.partial pre-configures constructors, and dataclasses with defaults replace many builders. Peter Norvig observed in 1996 that 16 of the 23 patterns become invisible or simpler in dynamic languages. The vocabulary still matters: saying 'this is an abstract factory' communicates intent in a code review faster than describing the mechanics.

A singleton guarantees one instance and global access to it. The second half is the problem: global access means any function can read or mutate shared state without declaring it, so dependencies hide, call order matters, and tests contaminate each other. Lazy initialization in threaded code adds races; Python's import lock makes module-level objects safe to create, while a hand-rolled check-then-create in __new__ is not atomic, a risk that grows on free-threaded builds.

Alternatives: create the object once at the composition root (main or app factory) and pass it in; use a module-level instance when truly global (the logging module does this); or use functools.cache on a factory function, which is easy to reset in tests with cache_clear(). Legitimate singletons exist: a process-wide connection pool, hardware handles, the None object itself. 'One instance' is fine; 'reachable from anywhere' is the smell.

In the GoF form, Factory Method is a template-method-style hook: the base class contains logic that needs an object, and subclasses override the creation step. The point is that export() stays unchanged while JsonExporter controls which writer it gets. In everyday Python, people usually mean a simple factory: a function or classmethod that picks a class, such as datetime.fromtimestamp or dict.fromkeys (alternative constructors).

A registry of classes keyed by string, often filled by a decorator, is the plugin-friendly version: new types register themselves without editing the factory, which satisfies open/closed. Pitfalls: string keys fail at runtime rather than at type-check time, and factories that return different types without a shared interface push isinstance checks back onto callers. Interview tip: the distinction between Factory Method (inheritance, one product) and Abstract Factory (composition, a family of products) is a common question.

Abstract Factory is an object with several creation methods whose products are designed to work together. The guarantee it gives is consistency: a client holding one factory cannot accidentally mix a dark button with a light menu, or an AWS queue with a GCP bucket client. It is usually implemented with one factory class per family, each made of factory methods.

The cost is rigidity in the other direction: adding a new product type (say, a tooltip) means changing the factory interface and every concrete factory. Adding a new family is cheap; adding a new product kind is expensive. This is the expression problem in miniature. In Python, a family can be a module (themes.dark, themes.light) or a dataclass of constructors. Dependency injection containers often play the abstract factory role at application scale.

Builder separates the construction steps from the final representation and allows validation once all parts are known. It shines when objects are immutable after creation, when some parameters depend on others, or when the same steps build different outputs (the GoF 'director' variant, such as one parser driving HTML and PDF builders).

Fluent builders return self from each step so calls chain; the final build() checks invariants, for example that a request with a body is not a GET. In Python, keyword-only arguments with defaults, dataclasses with __post_init__ validation, and pydantic models cover most cases without a separate builder class. Builders remain useful for query construction (SQLAlchemy select().where().order_by() is builder-like), test data builders that set only the fields a test cares about, and configuration assembled from several sources.

Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing, already configured one. It helps when construction is expensive (parsed config, loaded assets), when the class to create is only known through an existing instance, or when users design templates at runtime, such as game designers configuring enemy types.

In Python, copy.copy makes a shallow copy and copy.deepcopy copies recursively, tracking a memo dict to handle cycles. Classes can control both via __copy__ and __deepcopy__. Pitfalls: deep copies of objects holding file handles, locks or sockets fail or behave oddly; copied objects may share IDs that should be unique; and deep copying large graphs is slow. Immutable designs reduce the need entirely: with frozen dataclasses, dataclasses.replace(obj, hp=50) produces a modified copy safely, and sharing nested immutable parts is harmless.

A practical decision order: first ask whether a plain constructor call is enough, since most code needs no creational pattern. If the concrete type depends on runtime data, use a factory function or registry. If several created objects must stay consistent, group the creators into an abstract factory. If construction has many optional steps or needs validation across fields, use keyword arguments first, then a builder. If copying a configured instance is cheaper or simpler than building, use a prototype.

For 'there must be one', separate the two concerns: lifetime (one instance per process) is decided at the composition root; access should still be explicit through parameters. Patterns combine: a builder may use a prototype as its starting point, and abstract factories are often built from factory methods. Dependency injection frameworks automate factories and lifetimes (singleton, scoped, transient).

Pattern-itis is a real failure mode: an AbstractWidgetFactoryProvider for a single widget type adds names and indirection with no variation to justify them. Each creational pattern should point to an actual axis of change or a real construction problem.

Singleton damage is the most common: hidden coupling, order-dependent initialization, and tests that pass alone but fail together. Builders fail when build() does not validate, letting half-configured objects escape, or when the builder is mutable and reused accidentally across requests. Prototype bugs come from shallow copies sharing mutable state. Factories that swallow errors and return None hide failures. A good review question for any creational code: can a test create this object in one line with fakes, and can a reader find in one place where the concrete type is chosen?
swe-design-02.further: Read the original Design Patterns book selectively, then Norvig's 'Design Patterns in Dynamic Languages' talk to see which patterns Python absorbs. Study dependency injection and composition roots (Mark Seemann's work), object lifetimes in DI containers, and the expression problem. Learn Python specifics: classmethod alternative constructors, __init_subclass__ registries, entry points for plugins, dataclasses.replace and __deepcopy__. Brandon Rhodes' python-patterns guide is a strong Python-focused reference.

panels:
The GoF structural patterns are Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight and Proxy. Most rely on composition plus forwarding: an outer object holds an inner one and delegates. Because Adapter, Decorator and Proxy can have nearly identical code, the pattern name documents intent, which is the main reason to use the names in code review.

Python makes wrappers cheap. __getattr__ can forward any attribute not defined on the wrapper, which is handy but hides the interface from type checkers and IDEs, so explicit methods or a Protocol are clearer for public APIs. Flyweight, the one pattern not on this page, shares immutable state among many small objects to save memory; Python's interning of small ints and short strings, and __slots__, serve similar goals.

An adapter converts the interface of one class into the interface clients expect. Object adapters hold the adaptee (composition); class adapters inherit from it, which Python allows but couples you to its internals. Adapters are the standard way to isolate third-party SDKs: your domain code depends on your own small interface, and only the adapter imports the vendor library.

That isolation pays off in tests (fake the interface, not the SDK), in vendor migrations (write a second adapter) and in limiting blast radius when the SDK changes. Adapters should translate, not add business logic. Watch unit and type conversions, such as cents versus dollars: dividing by 100 gives a float, and money should usually stay in integer cents or Decimal to avoid rounding errors. In hexagonal architecture these are the 'driven adapters' plugged into ports.

A decorator wraps an object, keeps its interface and adds responsibilities before or after delegating. Because wrappers compose, n optional features need n classes instead of up to 2^n subclasses. Order matters: Retry(Cache(api)) retries cache misses, while Cache(Retry(api)) caches results after retries; logging outside a cache records hits too.

Python's @decorator syntax applies the same idea to functions: @f above def g is just g = f(g). Use functools.wraps so the wrapper keeps the name, docstring and signature. lru_cache is a built-in example; note that it holds strong references to arguments and results, and on methods it caches per self and can keep objects alive. Decorators should be transparent: a wrapper that changes return types or swallows exceptions breaks Liskov substitution for its callers.

A facade provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem without hiding the subsystem: advanced callers can still use the parts directly. It reduces coupling, since clients depend on one entry point, and it is a natural place for orchestration, ordering and error handling such as compensating actions (refund if shipping fails).

Service layers and application services in web backends are facades over repositories, payment and messaging. Client libraries often provide a facade over raw HTTP. The checkout example also hides an important design question: what happens on partial failure? Real systems use transactions, idempotency keys or sagas. The main risk is growth: a facade that accumulates every operation becomes a god object. Keep facades task-oriented, one per use case or area, and keep business rules in the domain rather than in the facade.

A proxy has the same interface as the real subject and controls access to it. Virtual proxies defer expensive creation (lazy loading); protection proxies check permissions; remote proxies make a network call look local (RPC stubs, gRPC clients); caching and smart-reference proxies add caching, reference counting or locking.

ORMs use virtual proxies for lazy-loaded relationships, which causes the N+1 query problem when a loop touches each relation and triggers one query per item. Remote proxies hide latency and partial failure, a classic fallacy of distributed computing, so make remote calls visible in names or types when it matters. Python examples: weakref.proxy, unittest.mock objects, and functools.cached_property for lazy attributes. Proxy versus decorator: both wrap; a proxy usually manages the subject's lifecycle or access, while a decorator adds behavior and is often stacked.

Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly through a shared component interface. Operations recurse: Folder.size() sums children, which may themselves be folders. Classic uses are file systems, UI widget trees, scene graphs, organization charts and abstract syntax trees.

Design choices: whether child-management methods (add, remove) belong on the shared interface (transparency, but leaves must reject them) or only on composites (safety, but callers need type checks). Recursion depth can hit Python's default limit of about 1000 frames on very deep trees, so iterative traversal with an explicit stack is safer for untrusted input. Cycles (symlinks, shared children) can cause infinite recursion; track visited nodes. Composite pairs naturally with Iterator for traversal and Visitor for adding operations without editing every node class.

Bridge decouples an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently, replacing a class explosion (m x n subclasses) with m + n classes connected by composition. The abstraction (Shape) holds a reference to an implementor (Renderer) and calls primitive operations on it, such as draw_circle(x, y, r).

It is often designed up front, unlike Adapter, which is usually retrofitted to make existing incompatible things work together. Real examples: database drivers behind a common API (Python's DB-API), logging handlers separate from loggers, and GUI toolkits separating widgets from platform backends. The hard part is defining the implementor interface: it must be rich enough for every abstraction yet implementable by every backend, a lowest common denominator problem. In Python, the implementor can simply be a function or object passed to the constructor, which makes Bridge look like Strategy; the intent differs (a structural split versus a swappable algorithm).

A quick intent test: if the wrapper exists because two interfaces do not match, it is an Adapter. If it adds behavior and keeps the interface, a Decorator. If it decides whether and when the real object is reached, a Proxy. If it offers a smaller, simpler interface over many objects, a Facade. Composite is about part-whole trees, Bridge about splitting two dimensions of variation.

Pitfalls beyond the two printed ones: wrappers can break identity and type checks (isinstance fails on a wrapped object), equality and hashing, and pickling. Deep wrapper stacks hurt performance in hot paths, since each layer adds a Python call costing tens of nanoseconds or more. Debugging gets harder when stack traces show many forwarding frames. Prefer a few named, well-tested wrappers, and document their order.
swe-design-03.further: Next, study Flyweight, the seventh structural pattern, and how Python's __slots__ and interning relate. Explore hexagonal architecture, where adapters and ports formalize these ideas, and the anti-corruption layer from domain-driven design. Learn functools.wraps, contextlib and descriptor-based proxies, plus wrapt for robust decorators. The N+1 query problem in ORMs, the fallacies of distributed computing for remote proxies, and the Visitor pattern for operations over composite trees are natural follow-ups.

panels:
Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and lets the caller choose. In Python the interface is usually just a callable signature, so a function, lambda, functools.partial or object with __call__ all qualify; sorted(key=...) and max(key=...) are built-in strategy parameters.

Use a class when the strategy carries configuration or state, or needs several related methods. Strategies are ideal for pricing rules, retry and backoff policies, compression or serialization formats, and ML components like optimizers or loss functions. The worked example also shows a subtle requirement: thresholds must be specified precisely. Free over 50 means a cart of exactly 50 still pays shipping with t > 50; if the business means 'from 50', the rule is t >= 50. Strategies make such rules easy to test in isolation with table-driven tests.

Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when the subject changes, it notifies registered observers. It decouples the subject from knowing who cares. Push style sends the data with the event; pull style sends a signal and observers query the subject.

Publish-subscribe is a related but distinct architecture: a broker or event bus sits in the middle, so publishers and subscribers do not know each other, and delivery may be asynchronous, persisted or cross-process (Kafka, Redis pub/sub). Pitfalls: the lapsed-listener problem, where a subject's list keeps dead observers alive (use weakref.WeakMethod or explicit unsubscribe); exceptions in one observer stopping others; reentrancy when an observer modifies the subject during notification; and unpredictable notification order. Iterate over a copy of the subscriber list if callbacks may unsubscribe themselves.

Command turns a request into an object containing everything needed to perform it later: the receiver, the action and the arguments. That reification enables queuing (task queues like Celery serialize commands), logging and replay, macro recording, transactional behavior, and undo/redo with two stacks: undo pops from history and pushes onto a redo stack; any new command clears the redo stack.

Undo design is the hard part. Either store enough state to reverse the action (inverse operations, like delete the inserted text) or store snapshots (Memento pattern), trading memory for simplicity. Commands sent over a network or retried must be idempotent or carry an idempotency key so duplicates do no harm. In CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) architectures, commands are the write side, kept separate from read-side queries.

State lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes, by delegating to a state object. Each state class implements the operations valid in that state and decides the transition, replacing scattered conditionals with explicit, testable classes. The object appears to change its class.

For simple cases, a transition table, a dict mapping (state, event) to next state, is often clearer than classes and can be validated or drawn as a diagram. Python's enum.Enum works well for state names. Explicit state machines matter for orders, payments, connections and protocol parsers, where invalid transitions (shipping an unpaid order) must be impossible rather than merely unlikely. Persisted state needs care: store the state name in the database, rebuild the state object on load, and guard transitions with optimistic locking to avoid two workers racing.

Template Method defines an algorithm's skeleton in a base class and defers some steps to subclasses. The base controls order and invariants; subclasses override hook methods. This is the Hollywood principle, 'don't call us, we'll call you', and it is how many frameworks work: unittest.TestCase calls your setUp, test methods and tearDown; Django class-based views call get_queryset and get_context_data.

The cost is inheritance coupling: subclasses depend on the base class's internal call order, and the fragile base class problem means changing the skeleton can break subclasses silently. Deep template hierarchies are hard to follow. The composition alternative passes the varying steps as functions or strategy objects, which is easier to test and combine. Mark required hooks with abc.abstractmethod so a missing override fails at instantiation rather than mid-run.

Iterator provides sequential access to elements without exposing the underlying representation. Python bakes it into the language: an iterable defines __iter__ returning an iterator, and an iterator defines __next__, raising StopIteration when done. for loops, comprehensions, unpacking and many built-ins use this protocol.

Generators are the easiest way to write iterators: yield suspends the function and keeps its local state, and yield from delegates to a sub-iterator. They are lazy, so they handle huge files or endless paginated APIs in constant memory. Pitfalls: iterators are single-pass, so a second loop over the same generator yields nothing; modifying a list or dict while iterating raises errors or skips elements; and laziness delays exceptions until consumption. The itertools module (islice, chain, groupby, batched in Python 3.12+) composes iterators efficiently.

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a sequence of handlers; each can handle it, reject it, or pass it on. The sender does not know which handler will act. Web middleware stacks (ASGI and WSGI middleware, Express-style) are the best-known example, along with logging handler hierarchies and event bubbling in UI trees.

Order is semantic: rate limiting before authentication protects the auth service from floods but limits anonymous traffic by IP rather than by user; logging first records rejected requests too. Each link should do one job. Failure modes include requests that fall off the end unhandled (add a default terminal handler), and expensive links placed early. A middleware that wraps the next call, as in ASGI, combines Chain of Responsibility with Decorator, since it can run code both before and after the rest of the chain.

Strategy versus State: same structure (delegation to an interchangeable object), different control. With Strategy, the client chooses and the strategy rarely changes during the object's life. With State, the context or the states themselves switch the current state as events arrive. Template Method versus Strategy: inheritance with a fixed skeleton versus composition with a swappable piece; prefer composition unless a framework hands you a base class.

Python simplifications: a one-method class can usually be a function, and a dict of functions often replaces a pattern class hierarchy. Hidden control flow is the main risk: observers that trigger other observers can form cascades or infinite loops, and chains and commands spread logic across many small files. Good tests, explicit names and a diagram in the docs keep these patterns understandable. Interviewers like asking which pattern a familiar API uses.
swe-design-04.further: Explore the remaining behavioral patterns: Mediator, Memento, Visitor and Interpreter. Learn reactive programming (ReactiveX) as Observer at scale, event sourcing and CQRS as Command at architectural scale, and statecharts (XState, the SCXML model) for complex state machines. In Python, study the iterator protocol in depth, generators, asyncio async iterators and itertools. Look at ASGI middleware internals to see Chain of Responsibility and Decorator combined.

panels:
Good names compress context: a reader should predict what a name holds or does without reading its body. Scope matters: a loop index i is fine in a three-line loop, while a module-level value needs a full descriptive name. Include units when ambiguity is costly: timeout_seconds, price_cents, distance_km. Functions are verbs (send_invoice), classes and values are nouns (Invoice), booleans are predicates (is_paid, has_access), and collections are plurals.

Consistency beats cleverness: pick one word per concept across the codebase and use the domain's language, which domain-driven design calls the ubiquitous language. Avoid encodings like Hungarian notation, misleading names (account_list that is a dict), and noise words (data, info, manager). PEP 8 conventions: snake_case for functions and variables, CapWords for classes, UPPER_CASE for constants. Renaming is the safest, most valuable refactoring; IDE rename tools make it nearly free.

Small functions are easier to name, test and reuse, but size is a proxy. The real goals are one level of abstraction per function (do not mix business steps with string parsing) and command-query separation: a function either changes state or returns information, not both. Step-down reading, where high-level functions call lower-level ones defined below, makes a module read like a narrative.

Too many tiny functions can fragment logic, forcing readers to jump around; John Ousterhout argues for deep modules with simple interfaces hiding significant functionality, a counterpoint to extreme splitting. Many parameters suggest the function does too much or that values belong together in an object. Boolean flag parameters often mean two functions in one: send(email, urgent=True) might be better as send_urgent(email). Use keyword-only arguments (def f(*, retries)) to keep call sites readable.

DRY, from The Pragmatic Programmer, is about knowledge, not text: every business rule should have a single, authoritative representation. Duplicated rules drift apart, and a bug fixed in one copy survives in another. Sandi Metz's warning applies too: 'duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction'. Removing duplication too early produces shared helpers full of flags and special cases.

KISS favors the simplest solution that meets current requirements; simplicity means few concepts and little coupling, not few characters. YAGNI, from Extreme Programming, rejects speculative generality: features, parameters and plugin systems built for needs that may never arrive cost code to maintain, tests to write and time not spent on real work. The rule of three balances these: tolerate a second copy, extract on the third, when the common shape is finally clear.

Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's implementation, not just its interface: changes to the base can break subclasses (the fragile base class problem), and combining features through subclassing explodes into many classes. The GoF book itself advises favoring object composition over class inheritance. Composition assembles behavior from parts held as attributes, which can be swapped at runtime and tested in isolation.

Inheritance is still right for genuine is-a relationships with stable contracts, for framework extension points, and for abstract base classes defining interfaces. Python adds mixins, small classes adding one capability via multiple inheritance; they work but rely on method resolution order (MRO), and cooperative super() calls get tricky. Rule of thumb: inherit interfaces, compose implementations. Protocols give polymorphism without any inheritance, so 'is-a' can often become 'behaves-like'.

Dependency injection means an object receives its collaborators instead of constructing or looking them up. Constructor injection is the default; parameter injection (as with greet(clock=...)) suits functions; setter injection allows late wiring but permits half-initialized objects. Wiring happens at the composition root, usually main() or an app factory.

Typical injected dependencies are the nondeterministic or slow ones: clocks, random generators, HTTP clients, databases, file systems and environment configuration. Injecting them makes tests fast and deterministic without monkeypatching. Python frameworks offer built-in DI, such as FastAPI's Depends and pytest fixtures. A detail in the printed example: datetime.now as a default is safe because the function object is evaluated once, not called at definition time, unlike the classic bug def f(t=datetime.now()), which freezes the time when the module loads. Avoid service locators, which hide dependencies again.

A code smell, a term from Kent Beck and Martin Fowler's Refactoring, is a surface symptom that often indicates a deeper design problem; it is a prompt to look, not proof of a bug. Fowler's catalog pairs smells with named moves. Others worth knowing: feature envy (a method uses another class's data more than its own -> Move Function), data clumps (the same three fields travel together -> Extract Class), primitive obsession (strings for emails and money -> value objects), shotgun surgery (one change touches many files -> consolidate), and divergent change (one class changes for many reasons -> split).

Replace Conditional with Polymorphism is the bridge to the Strategy and State patterns. Linters and analyzers such as ruff, pylint and radon (cyclomatic complexity) detect some smells automatically; complexity above roughly 10 per function is a common warning threshold.

Fowler defines refactoring as a change to internal structure that leaves observable behavior unchanged. The safety net is a fast test suite: run it after each step, and if it fails, revert rather than debug, because the step was small. Commit at every green point so any step can be undone, and keep refactoring commits separate from behavior changes so reviewers can check each kind on its own terms.

For legacy code without tests, Michael Feathers' approach: find seams, write characterization tests that assert current outputs (even wrong ones), then refactor. Snapshot and approval testing speed this up. For large changes, use the strangler fig pattern or branch by abstraction to migrate gradually behind an interface while the system keeps working, and parallel change (expand, migrate, contract) for APIs and database schemas. Automated IDE refactorings are safer than manual edits.

Big-bang rewrites fail often because the old system encodes years of undocumented edge cases, and the new one must catch up with a moving target while delivering no value until cutover. Incremental replacement, as with the strangler fig, keeps value flowing and limits risk.

Other pitfalls: wrong abstractions created by over-zealous DRY; refactoring without tests, which is just changing code; mixing formatting changes into functional diffs, which hides real changes in review (run formatters in a separate commit); and refactoring code that is about to be deleted. Cleverness costs readers time; prefer obvious code even if longer. Comments should explain why, such as constraints, trade-offs and links to tickets, while names and structure explain what. Track refactoring as part of normal work, following the Boy Scout rule, rather than as a separate phase that never gets scheduled.
swe-design-05.further: Read Fowler's Refactoring (2nd edition) for the full smell and move catalog, Feathers' Working Effectively with Legacy Code for seams and characterization tests, and Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design for deep modules as a counterpoint to tiny functions. Explore the strangler fig pattern, parallel change, mutation testing to check test strength, and static analysis tools such as ruff, mypy and radon. Sandi Metz's talks on the wrong abstraction and on composition are short, practical follow-ups.
